final_note: Lag time and peak discharge reveal basin response.

walkthroughs.body_html: Annual UK precipitation averages about 1150 mm; evapotranspiration about 400 mm; the rest becomes runoff and groundwater recharge. Soil moisture deficit develops in summer when evapotranspiration exceeds rainfall.

Flashy hydrographs (short lag, high peak) occur in urbanised, impermeable basins. Subdued hydrographs (long lag, low peak) characterise vegetated, permeable basins. Urbanisation in the Don catchment, Sheffield reduced lag from hours to minutes.

The Tees rises on impermeable Carboniferous millstone grit in Cumbria. Cow Green Reservoir regulates flow. Storm Desmond (2015) brought 341 mm in 24 hours to Honister Pass, producing record peak flows and flooding Carlisle.

mcqs.q: What is lag time on a storm hydrograph?
options: It is the process of rain falling from clouds.
The time between peak rainfall and peak river discharge — affected by drainage basin shape, land use, soil saturation and vegetation.
Lag time is how long the storm itself lasts.
Lag time is the delay between thunder and lightning.
It is the process of rain falling from clouds.
Humans affect the carbon cycle by eating plants.
The combined loss of water from a surface through evaporation (from soil and water bodies) and transpiration (from plant leaves).
It is only water evaporating from puddles and lakes.

mcqs.q: How do humans affect the carbon cycle?
options: Humans only affect the carbon cycle by breathing out CO2.
By burning fossil fuels (releasing stored geological carbon to the atmosphere) and deforestation (reducing the biosphere store and releasing carbon).
Humans affect the carbon cycle by eating plants.
It is the process of rain falling from clouds.
